explanation: Fires on abstract head nouns like 'aspect(s)', 'concerns', 'importance' that come right after a modifying adjective or noun ('biological aspects', 'safety concerns', 'critical importance'). It fires more weakly on 'of' in 'one of' and on 'been' after 'has/have'. The top hit is a stray Chinese token, so there is some unrelated noise.

Fires on word-piece tokens in the middle of a word in Romance-language text (Portuguese, Spanish, Italian, French), especially the opening piece of a word at the start of a sentence ('Est|ou', 'J|'ai', 'quier|o'). It is weak on English and fires only modestly on code or legal boilerplate tokens such as '="' or 'FOR'.

Fires on the first word-piece of a word that is split into pieces, usually a capitalized proper name or a rare technical word ('R|otten', 'P|ondering', 'gl|aucoma', 'P|wC', 'P|appas'). P and G pieces are especially common. It does not fire on whole common words.

Fires on an opening quotation mark (" “ ') that brings in a named term or phrase after framing words like 'called', 'known as', 'defined as', 'the term' or 'or'. Closing quotes and quotes that open dialogue are much weaker. There are occasional offshoots on sports words like 'tiebreaker' or 'round'.

Fires on tokens inside formulaic abbreviation or reference markup: the 'ref'/'B' inside citation brackets like [@B3] or [@ref6], degree abbreviations ('B.S', 'M.Sc', "Bachelor's"), and boilerplate pieces like 'BSD-style', 'namespace' and 'android.com'. In ordinary prose it is only moderate or weak.

Fires on word-pieces that begin with 'w' or 'sw' (also 'tw', 'unw', 'W'), such as '-w|inner', '-w|ed', 'w|ok', 'sw|arms', 'sw|ine', 'Magick|W|and', 'D|w|elling'. It fires whether the piece starts the word or sits in the middle. Other letters fire only weakly.

A mixture with no single theme. It fires on code and technical tokens (C macro pieces like O_NONBLOCK and m_Double, 'avformat_open', compiler error colons, license boilerplate), on the word-pieces 'bur' in 'outbursts' and 'ol' in 'phospholipid', on 'a' in technical Q&A prose, and on some Chinese tokens.

Fires on scattered tokens with no shared meaning: HTML/SQL attribute names, digits inside numbers or years, periods after initials, 'of' in category names and set phrases, plus assorted content words. No clear rule predicts it.

Fires mainly on philosophy and academic-theory contexts: 'philosopher', 'philo', 'deconstructionist', 'Georg' Simmel, and prepositions in abstract or theoretical prose. It also fires on 'Ph'/'PH'/'ph' letter pieces ('Ph.D', 'PHIL', 'epiphany', '-phobia'), which looks like a spelling offshoot.

Fires strongly on 'of' when it links a noun phrase to the whole or entity that the noun belongs to or describes ('the imperfections of', 'method of the Calendar class', 'components of LibreOffice', 'the solubility of'). Other prepositions such as 'in', 'for', 'at' and 'the' are only weak or moderate.

Fires on commas and on 'in' at clause boundaries in formal legal, patent and scientific prose, especially right after a passive or participle verb or a clause like 'is known' or 'denied by the trial court', and in set phrases such as 'relates, in general,' or 'in particular'. Casual text is weak.

Fires on fairly generic function words or sentence openers in news and web prose: 'any', 'in' (as in '$11 million in'), 'a', 'Sometimes', 'Often', 'Consequently', closing parentheses after names. No clear common trigger.

Fires in biographical and sports-encyclopedia text about schools, colleges and teams, on tokens that lead into a team, league or institution name ('basketball for', 'minor league', 'As a senior', 'All-Sunshine', 'Big Ten', 'graduated from'). It fires more weakly on place-name pieces such as 'N' in NMSU or 'N.D. Texas'.

Fires on words that introduce a list of examples or members: 'such as' (on 'as'), 'including', 'include', 'namely', 'the first' in 'Two examples are given: the first'. 'like' and 'For example,' are moderate.

A mixture: it fires on 'you' in 'Can you', on 'half' in 'the second/first half (of)', on 'relative' in 'relative to', on CamelCase identifier pieces in code imports ('.OnClickListener', 'ZonedDateTime', '.viewDidLoad'), and on assorted words such as 'NATO'.

Fires in code on array or collection indexing: the '[' just before an index or the collection name before '[i]' ('str[0]', 'names[i]', '.split(',')[0]'), plus nearby declaration or pointer tokens in C, JS or Go. Code with no indexing context is weak.

Fires on early word-pieces of unusual proper names and rare words, often names beginning with K, I, Rak/ak or 'le' ('re|k|ognition', 'KE|W', 'Ale|k|sey', 'I|liamna', 'Mal|ala', '-le|ader'). The pattern is broad and loose.

Fires on word-pieces inside rare or technical words and names, especially Greek or Latin prefix pieces ('monoc' in monoclonal, 'poly', 'quadr', 'pur', 'cris') and pieces of names ('Will|ough|by', 'Schleswig-H|olstein', 'Ro|java'). Common whole words are weak.

Fires on the first word-piece of a split word that begins with a prefix-like or Romance stem ('dis|ench|anted', 'ass|urer', 'rec|upero', 'ré|duit', 'AP|PEALS', 'Ab|strium'), in French, Italian, English and code text. The whole word must be split into pieces.

Fires on the token that ends a citation or number just before closing punctuation: the closing ']' of citation markers like [@B6], the last digit of years and numbers before a period or comma, and the final word of a sentence before its period ('License', 'said', a surname).

Fires on the surname, especially its later word-pieces, in a person's full name ('Fryk|man', 'B|ROWN', 'Sw|enson', 'Mark Taylor'). It is strongest in news, legal or sports bylines and attributions. First names and non-name words do not fire.
